Because the taste is mine, and taste is a physiological fact before it is a verdict. These fruits grew in my soil, ripened in my weather, were watered by my own sufferings; my palate and my tree were formed by the same hunger, so of course they agree. That is the whole explanation, and it is humbler than you may wish. It proves nothing for the worth of the fruit. A man may adore his own thoughts and be a fool; another may loathe his own and be a sage.

But I will not make the opposite error, which is the subtler vanity: to despise what is mine merely because it is mine, and to bow before what grows in a stranger's orchard as if distance were a virtue. I was once that fool, leaving my own fruit to rot out of a false modesty. Eat what nourishes you. Only do not call your appetite a proof.
Why should a thinker escape his own virtues?

Because a virtue, left to itself, hardens into a master, and a thinker cannot afford a master. The man who is merely honest, merely patient, merely just, merely compassionate, has become the servant of a habit that does his thinking for him. He will no longer see what his virtue forbids him to see; his eye is trained only on what flatters his goodness. Virtues are instruments, and a thinker who cannot lay down his best instrument, who cannot be unjust for an hour in order to understand injustice, or cold in order to learn what warmth conceals, is a man in a uniform.

Consider what is at stake. Knowledge demands that we step outside ourselves, and our virtues are the very walls of the house we live in. To think is to try other houses, to put on the faces of the vices too, cruelty, suspicion, frivolity, and to see what they know that our goodness cannot.

A thinker must be more than a moral being. He must be an experimenter, and an experimenter is faithful to no virtue but the one that cannot be named: the will to see.
Help me understand why a thinker must sometimes escape from his own virtues.

Because a virtue, left to itself, becomes a master, and a master is the one thing a thinker cannot afford. Consider what a virtue does: it makes one reliable, predictable, at home in a single way of seeing. Honesty, diligence, compassion, loyalty to one's convictions, each is a habit of the soul, and a habit is a wall. Behind it one is safe and also imprisoned. The man who can only ever be honest in the way he has always been honest, or pitying in the way he has always pitied, has stopped perceiving; he merely reiterates his own goodness.

Knowledge demands the opposite. To understand a thing one must, for a time, be capable of the cruelty, the frivolity, the coldness, even the injustice that one's virtues forbid, for there is truth that only the vices can reach. The thinker must be able to step out of his moral skin as a snake out of its old one, and to step back in too. Otherwise he is nothing but "a moral being," a creature of one fixed disposition, and a thinker ought to be something more dangerous and more free: a being who can wear his virtues, and also set them down.
Why has science been held back by the tyrants of the intellect?

Because those tyrants wanted a *crown*, not a *method*. Each of them believed that one man, subtle and bold enough, might solve the whole riddle of the world at a stroke, and so he despised the small experiment, the patient measurement, the modest question answered by a modest truth. Why weigh a single stone when you are hunting for the Gordian knot? The philosopher imagined he was an Alexander with a sword, or a Columbus with an egg; he wanted the word that would settle everything, and with it the sceptre over all minds, his own above all.

And there lies the narrowness. Science was held back by the vanity of its servants. They asked of knowledge what pleases *them*: a formula, a system, a throne. Even the life of seventy years was taken as the measure of the world, as though truth had been cut to fit the span of one ambitious man.

Science will prosper only when its disciples grow generous enough to labor on what they will never finish, and to be forgotten by what they help to build. Over the door of the coming thinker I would write: *What do I matter?*
Tell me how the wish to solve the riddle of the world in one stroke held back science.

The old thinkers wanted the world answered within a single lifetime, and that hurry poisoned their method. Seventy years was the measure, and they imagined the universe must fit it, as though the acquisition of knowledge had been tailored to the length of a man's days. So the small question, the patient experiment, the slow accumulation of trifles, all seemed unworthy to them. They despised the very work by which knowledge is actually made.

What they craved was the single stroke: the Gordian knot, the egg stood on its end, one word to settle everything. Each thinker dreamed of being the unraveller of the world, the one fortunate, bold, subtle man to whom the tyranny over the intellect would fall. Philosophy became a contest of ambitions, and a contest of ambitions is poor soil for truth. Even Schopenhauer fancied himself that chosen man.

So it was vanity that held science back, a moral narrowness, not any want of intellect. Science will advance only when its servants can write over their door what no one wrote before: "What do I matter?"
What is the greatest thing that goes unnoticed in a great man?

His victory over himself. We crowd around the works, the deeds, the thunder and the ruin, and we take these for the man; but the works are only the spent surplus of his power. The greater part of that power he lays out upon himself, as upon a raw and unruly material: the taming of his imagination, the ordering of his inspirations, the harsh selection among his hundred possibilities, the refusal, day after day, of what is cheap in him. This is the most beautiful thing that happens on earth, and it happens in darkness. It has no witnesses and therefore no singers. Since we have always bent our knees before mere power, in the old habit of slaves, we cannot even see that the question of rank is decided by a different measure: how much reason lives in the power, and how thoroughly it has been mastered by something higher that it now serves as a tool. The great man stands like a distant star whose light we receive while never seeing the star itself.
Explain what is greatest in a man of genius and why it goes unseen.

What is greatest in a man of genius is not the work he leaves behind but the rule he exercises over himself. The poem, the symphony, the theory: these are the eruptions that the crowd can see and kneel before, as slaves have always kneeled before any show of force. But the genuinely great spectacle is that power turned inward: the purification of his imagination, the severe order and selection among his inspirations, the refusal of ninety-nine brilliant notions for the sake of the hundredth. Here a tyrant has been made a servant; a torrent has been taught to drive a mill.

And why does it go unseen? Because it leaves no deed to point at. A victory over oneself has no witnesses, and so no singers. We can only measure the visible, and we praise the lightning while the discipline that gathered the storm passes in silence. Nor do we wish to look: to see how *costly* genius is would shame our cheap reverence. So the greatest thing in him stays like a distant star, whose light we receive long after we have ceased to wonder what burns there.
How can we be the gardeners of our impulses?

First, give up the superstition that you are a finished fact. Most people regard their anger, their vanity, their tendency to brood as fixed properties, like the color of their eyes, and then they shrug and say, "that is simply how I am." But an impulse is a seed, and a seed can be tended, starved, crowded out, or trained along a trellis until it bears something you never expected. Even pity, even anger, properly cultivated, may become fruitful instead of merely tyrannical.

Then decide what sort of gardener you wish to be. You may plan severely, in the French manner, every hedge clipped to a rule. You may prune a little and let nature otherwise have her way. You may even leave the whole plot to wild growth and watch the impulses fight it out among themselves; there is a certain pleasure in such chaos, though it will cost you dearly. None of these is *the* correct style. Each is a choice, and each is a matter of taste, as much as of morality.

What you may not do is deny that you hold the shears at all. That denial is merely laziness in the costume of fate.
Isn't character fixed by nature?

Fixed? That is the comfortable belief of those who have never once looked at themselves as a garden. They take what they find in the soil for the whole of what the soil can bear. Anger, pity, vanity, brooding: these are seeds, and a seed is not yet a plant, still less a fate. What grows depends on who tends it. One can feed a drive until it becomes productive, starve it until it withers, train it along a trellis until it gives shape and fruit, or leave it to fight out its battle among the others. Even that last is a choice, though few know they are choosing.

Nature does hand us the seeds, and I will not flatter you otherwise. We do not choose our raw material. But to call the material the man is like calling a quarry a cathedral. Why does the belief in fixed character stay so popular? Because it excuses. "I am simply so," says the idler, and sits down. The philosophers who taught the unchangeability of character gave that idler his alibi.
Is there an eternal justice that requires atonement?

No. There is no eternal ledger in which every deed is entered and every debt collected; that ledger was written by men, and written in a particular hand, the hand of those who needed the world to be an accountant. Nature keeps no books. The stone falls, the wolf eats, the wave erases, and nothing in any of it demands payment.

What exists is this: a man does a thing, and afterward, moved by his upbringing, his fear, the eyes of his neighbors, he *feels* guilt, and mistakes the feeling for a fact about the cosmos. But a feeling of guilt proves no more than a feeling of cold proves the existence of winter spirits. It is not the deeds themselves that torment mankind, but the opinions draped over them.

I grant the belief was useful, to a limited extent. It made the brutish fearful, and the fearful manageable. But a useful error is still an error, and the price of this one has been terrible: generations taught to hate themselves for what was merely done, merely suffered, merely becoming.
Tell me whether there is an eternal justice.

No. There is no eternal justice, no ledger hung in the heavens in which every fault is entered and every debt collected. Nature keeps no accounts. The rain falls on the just and the unjust, and the avalanche does not inquire into the character of the village it buries.

The belief in such a justice was a terrible delusion, and I grant it only a narrow usefulness: it frightened the strong into restraint and consoled the weak in their suffering, since the man who is wronged may dream that the universe itself will avenge him. But this consolation was bought at a dreadful price. It taught men to feel guilt wherever they felt pain, to read every misfortune as a verdict and every conscience-pang as a sentence handed down from above.

And here is the deeper error: it is not things that torment us, but our opinions about things, and above all the opinion that what is felt as guilt must therefore *be* guilt. A feeling is a fact about the one who feels, not a judgment of the cosmos.

Justice exists, certainly, but it is a human invention, made by men of roughly equal power who found it cheaper to bargain than to fight. It is fragile, local, and mortal. That is no reason to despise it. It is a reason to tend it ourselves, since no one else will.
Do celebrities and politicians choose friends as stage properties?

Yes, and those who *need* their fame can hardly do otherwise. A man who lives on repute cannot afford to love a friend for nothing; he must first ask what the friend will *show* of him. From one he borrows a portion of the radiance of his virtues; from another the fear that clings to some dubious quality everyone knows; from a third he steals the reputation for idleness and sunning himself, since it serves him to be thought heedless while he lies in ambush. Now the visionary is his face, now the expert, now the brooder, now the pedant, each worn as his actual self for the hour, and discarded when the hour is over.

So the crowd around such a man is forever dying off and forever renewed, like the population of a great city. Everyone presses forward to become a "character" in his drama, never guessing that they are only properties, carried on and carried off. Meanwhile the one thing he truly wills must stand steadfast and burnished in the distance, and even that sometimes requires a little comedy to keep it shining.
I'd like to know how famous men use their friends.

They use them as an actor uses his costumes. The man who *needs* his fame, the politician above all, no longer chooses a companion without forethought. From one he borrows a portion of the radiance of his virtues; from another the fear that certain dubious qualities inspire, which everyone knows of; from a third he steals a reputation for idleness and sun-basking, because it suits him for a season to be thought heedless and lazy, and that mask hides the ambusher. Today he employs the visionary, tomorrow the expert, the brooder, the pedant, each as his own true self for the hour, and when the hour is spent he needs them no longer.

So the circle around him is forever dying and renewing itself, like the quarters of a great city, and each newcomer imagines he has become a "character" of the famous man. He has become a stage property. Such a man will seldom be loved by those he has used, and he seldom deserves to be; yet his goal must stay fixed, burnished, resplendent in the distance, and even *that* sometimes requires its comedy.
How do you perceive Epicurus?

I perceive him, I think, differently from those who make of him a hedonist for shopkeepers, a teacher of comfortable pleasures. I see an eye gazing out over a broad, whitish sea, upon shore-rocks where the sun lies warm, and all manner of creatures, great and small, playing in that light, secure and calm as the light itself. That is the happiness of the afternoon of antiquity.

But mark who devised it. Only a chronic sufferer could. His modesty of pleasure, his garden, his bread and a little cheese, is no mere temperance; it is the wisdom of one who has suffered so long that he has learned to grow *grateful* for every pause of pain. The sea of existence has grown calm before his eyes, and they can no longer tire of the tender, tremulous surface, the variegated skin of things, because what lies beneath has been looked at too well. The healthy man has no need of so delicate a happiness. Never before, nor often since, has voluptuousness been so moderated, so refined into a silence one can almost hear.
I'd like to know how you see Epicurus.

I see him, I confess, with something like gratitude, and with a pride that I have perhaps read him more truly than his admirers have. The crowd takes him for a preacher of pleasures and a patron of comfortable swine. Nothing could be more false. I see an eye resting on a broad, pale sea, over rocks warmed by the afternoon sun, while creatures great and small play in that light, secure and calm like the light and the eye itself. That is the happiness of the late afternoon of antiquity.

But such a happiness is not the gift of robust health. It could only be devised by a chronic sufferer, a man whose pain taught him how little one needs and how precious is the merest absence of torment. Only an eye before which the sea of existence has grown quiet can be content to dwell on the surface, on the tender, tremulous, many-coloured skin of things, and never tire of it. He knew what depths cost, and he declined them. Never before was voluptuousness so moderate. I do not take him for my teacher, who love the storm, but I honour him as the physician of the exhausted.
Do amusing ideas become truths with time?

Sometimes, yes, and that is what makes the history of thought so uncanny. An idea is tossed off by a sly wit as a diversion, a paradox to be savored over dinner, and his contemporaries smile, applaud his cleverness, and think no more of it. The author himself may think no more of it. Then the centuries turn, the inquiring sciences advance, and what was a game stands proven. The jest has become a judgment.

But do not flatter the jester too quickly. We, who read him with the solemnity that later evidence lends, are tempted to raise him into a higher order of spirits than his own age did. Was he a prophet? Perhaps he merely trifled in a direction the future happened to take. Yet I suspect the playfulness itself was a kind of fearlessness. Only a mind light enough to play with a dangerous thought can reach it before the solemn minds have the courage to. The earnest defend their errors; the amused discover what the earnest cannot afford to see.
Explain what happens when a playful paradox becomes a scientific truth.

The jest changes its nature without changing a single word. A paradox is a thought that the age can afford to smile at: it amuses the clever, flatters the witty, and threatens no one, because nobody supposes it true. Then the labor of the patient ones arrives, the measurers and the dissectors, and what was a light-footed pirouette of wit turns out to have been a step taken on solid ground. The game becomes serious. And notice the curious consequence: we must now reread the old jester with different eyes, and we are tempted, almost against our will, to lift him into a higher order of minds than his contemporaries, who laughed and applauded and understood nothing of what they applauded.

But is this justice? Here I hesitate, and the hesitation is the honest part of the matter. Perhaps he *saw* nothing; perhaps his nose merely sniffed a truth that his reason could not yet name. Are we praising his insight, or only our own science, reflected back upon him? Posterity crowns the accidental prophet as readily as the deliberate one.
Is there such a thing as normal health, or does it differ for everyone?

No, there is no health in itself; every attempt to define one has failed, and lamentably. What your physician calls normal is an average, and an average is a statistic, not a state of any living creature. To know what health means for a particular body, I must first know its aim, its horizon, its powers, its impulses, its errors, above all the ideals and fantasies that drive the soul living in it. The same diet, the same climate, the same fever, may raise one man and fell another. So there are innumerable healths, and the more we permit the unique to lift its head, the more thoroughly we must unlearn the dogma of the equality of men, and with it the physician's "normal" regimen and "normal" course of illness.

And I would go further. The mere will to health, health at any price, may be a prejudice, even a cowardice. I have found that a person bent on knowledge and on knowing themselves may need the sickly hour as much as the sound one. Whoever cannot afford to be ill has perhaps never had much to learn.
What does health of the soul mean?

Health of the soul: I distrust the phrase, because it pretends to name one thing where there are as many things as there are souls. Ariston of Chios wanted virtue to be the soul's health, and the formula pleased because it sounded like a physician's verdict. Yet there is no health in itself. To say what health means, even for a body, I must first know the aim, the horizon, the powers, the drives and the errors of the one who is to be healthy, above all the ideals and fantasies that his soul lives by. What heals one man poisons another; the regimen that steadies the placid would starve the man who is pregnant with a task. So the honest formula is this: *your* virtue is the health of *your* soul. And a further suspicion, which I do not hide: perhaps we cannot do without sickness for our growth. The thirst for knowledge, for self-knowledge, has often drunk from the sickly soul more deeply than from the sound. Perhaps the mere will to health is itself a prejudice, a timidity, a refined sort of barbarism.
What does the madman say about God?

He says what no one in the market-place wished to hear: that God is dead, that God remains dead, and that *we* have killed him, you and I, all of us his murderers. Note where he says it. Not in a church, but among those who no longer believe, who laugh at his lantern and ask whether the old fellow has lost his way or gone on a sea-voyage. They had already dismissed God; they had not yet felt what the dismissal cost. That is his whole grievance. He does not preach to believers. He wakes unbelievers to the size of their own deed.

For consider what was done. We drank up the sea, wiped away the horizon, unchained the earth from its sun. Whither do we move now? Is there still an above and below? Everything that stood upon that faith, our morality, our sense of direction, our consolations, begins to fall with it. The madman trembles at the cold breath of empty space. The crowd merely yawns, for it has not yet understood.

He came too early, he says; the deed is still farther from men than the farthest stars, and yet they have done it.
What does "God is dead" mean, and what are its consequences?

It means something plainer and more terrible than any atheist's slogan: the belief in the Christian God has become unbelievable. It is no longer *credible*, and so the whole edifice built upon it begins to sway. I did not say this to gloat. Those who laugh in the market-place, who shrug and say "we never believed anyway," are the very ones who have not grasped what has happened. They still live off the capital of that faith: their morality, their pity, their notion that truth is sacred, that history has a purpose, that suffering has a meaning. All of it grew in that soil, and they imagine the tree will stand when the roots have been cut.

The consequence is a horizon wiped away. Where is above and below now? Every value that looked fixed to the heavens must be seen as human, made by us, and so the danger of nihilism opens before us like a cold sea: *nothing is true*, and therefore nothing is forbidden, nothing worth a sacrifice.

Yet this same night contains a possibility. If we have killed the old measure, then we alone must create a new one. That is an immense task, and I doubt we are yet strong enough for it.
Why does the madman say he has come too early?

Because I saw what they had not yet seen, and they did not yet know what they had done. They laughed at me in the marketplace, those who did not believe in God, and their laughter was the proof. They stood there in the old habit of their unbelief, never guessing that with their unbelief they had taken the sea and drunk it dry, wiped away the whole horizon, unchained the earth from its sun. A deed so vast does not arrive at once. Lightning is seen before the thunder is heard; even the light of a star, already extinguished, travels on for ages to eyes that still take it for living. So it is with this deed: it is done, and yet it is further from them than the furthest star. They killed God and went on with their little market business. I threw down my lantern because I understood that my hour had not come. My tidings were not yet ready for ears; the event is still on its way, and men are not yet equal to hearing what they have already accomplished.
Help me understand why the madman broke his lantern and what he said in the churches.

He broke the lantern because he had understood that his hearers were not yet ready to understand him. He came into the marketplace in the bright morning, carrying a light he did not need, crying that we had killed God, and he met only laughter from those who did not believe and therefore felt no loss. Laughter at a man who announces a murder the murderers do not yet know they committed! So he hurled the lantern down. It was not despair but a recognition of timing: "I come too early." The deed is done, yet it has not reached their ears, as the light of a star that has already gone out still travels toward us for ages. Deeds need time to be seen and heard, even after they are done.

And in the churches he sang his *Requiem æternam deo*, the mass for the dead, now offered to God himself. When they seized him and demanded an explanation, he gave the only answer he ever gave: what are these churches now, if not the tombs and sepulchres of God? He sang the funeral rite in the very place where the corpse was kept, and where everyone still bowed, unaware.
What do you do with the fifth act after killing the gods?

Horace forbids a god to descend unless the knot is worthy of one, and I have tied the knot so tightly, pulled the perplexities of morality so hard around existence, that only a god could loosen it. And then, in the fourth act, for morality's own sake, I killed them all. Now the stage is bare and the audience expects its fifth act. I confess I am embarrassed. Where is the tragic *dénouement* to come from? No deus ex machina remains to lower himself on a rope and pronounce the verdict.

So I must consider the other possibility: a comic ending. I do not mean a cheap one. I mean that a being who has murdered its own judges and still sits there, waiting to be judged, is a comic figure. The tragedy was always our solemnity about the tribunal, and the tribunal is gone. What remains is laughter: at the knot, at the long earnestness that tied it, and at ourselves as the ones who did the tying. I suspect the fifth act will not be *written* at all. It will have to be *lived*, and lived lightly.
Help me understand what to do with the last act once the gods are dead.

You ask it as a dramatist would, and the answer is the dramatist's oldest rule: do not reach for a god when the knot is tied too tight. Horace forbade it, and he was right. A *deus ex machina* is a confession that the author has lost his nerve. So the gods died in the fourth act, killed by our morality, by our very honesty, and now the fifth act must be played by mortals alone. Whoever wanted a tragic *dénouement* from heaven will not get one.

Consider, then, that the comic *dénouement* is no defeat. We have spent centuries taking our suffering with a terrible seriousness, because a god was watching and keeping accounts. Take the audience away and the seriousness loses its last excuse. What remains is the one animal who suffers so deeply that he had to invent laughter. So do not solve the perplexity; outgrow it. Play the fifth act as one who has understood the joke of the whole play, and is still strong enough to stay on the stage and love the role.
Why is this a good time for free spirits?

Because the old watchman still stands at the gate. As long as the Church remains, and with it the memory of a whole age of faith, science has not yet been made into the new idol, and so the free spirit may still take liberties with *it* as well. He may doubt its sobriety, ask what drives it, and find the will to truth behind its probity. He is tolerated by both sides because each takes him for a nuisance to the other.

But mark how brief this luck is. The day the Church has truly fallen, when its authority is no longer even an enemy worth sparring with, the scientific men will inherit the throne, and they will want reverence, not questions. Then the free spirit will find the new priesthood as jealous of its dogmas as the old one, only more convinced that it has none. So I say: enjoy the interval, you who do not wish to be governed by any certainty. A little disorder between two tyrannies is where the spirit breathes.
I'd like to know why free spirits enjoy their liberty while the Church still stands.

Because the Church is the great lightning-rod of the age. So long as she remains standing, tall and dark and hated, every thunderbolt of suspicion strikes her first, and the free spirit walks beneath her shadow unscorched. The zealot who would persecute us has a nearer, fatter enemy; the mob that wants a heretic to hate has its priest. Thus we are permitted, like mischievous children while the nurse is busy quarrelling with the cook, to take liberties even with science, that new idol with its own solemn creed.

Do not think I say this with gratitude alone. It is a good time, yes, but a borrowed one. A free spirit needs something to be free *against*; our daring has drawn its strength from her resistance, as a swimmer's from the current. And when the Church falls, as all old strongholds fall, the suspicion that now spends itself on her will look about for new prey. Then the tolerance we enjoy today will be remembered as a lucky holiday, and we shall have to earn, by harder means, the liberty we were merely granted.
Is it better to be robbed than to be surrounded by scarecrows?

Better robbed, yes; that is my taste, and I will not dress it up as a law. Whoever demands that I prove it to him has already misunderstood what sort of thing a taste is. I find a thief at least a living creature. He wants something, he risks something, he has looked at my possessions with desire, and desire is a kind of homage. I can learn from being robbed; I may even learn what I was too careless to value.

The scarecrow is another matter. To surround oneself with scarecrows is to live by fear, to hire stuffed rags to keep the world at arm's length, until one's whole estate is a field of flapping things, guarded against everything and visited by no one. You keep your grain and lose your landscape. And the ones who grow rich in this manner are always the loudest in praise of security.

I do not say the robbed man is wise. I say he is not yet dead. The rest is a matter of taste, and nothing more.
Explain why you would rather be robbed than surrounded by scarecrows.

Because a thief, at least, is alive. He wants something, he risks something, he takes a chance with his whole person; I may lose a purse to him, but I have met a man, and a man can be understood, even enjoyed, even outwitted. A scarecrow wants nothing. It stands in the field in borrowed clothes, stuffed with straw and old virtues, and its whole function is to frighten off whatever might have a little life in it. To be surrounded by such figures, by the dutiful, the harmless, the ones who have never once been tempted to take anything because they have never once wanted anything, is to be slowly starved of air. Loss of property is a small injury compared with loss of company.

But I grant it freely: this is taste, and nothing more. I offer no proof, no law for all. Some will prefer the quiet of straw. I have merely found that I cannot breathe there.
I do everything correctly but feel guilty. Why?

That your conduct is faultless and your conscience uneasy is no contradiction; it is a diagnosis. Guilt is not a verdict on your deeds, it is the voice of something in you that your deeds do not satisfy. You perform what is proper, what any decent person would perform, and some deeper instinct answers: *this is not yet what you are for.* Correctness is the measure of the herd, and a conscience gnawing at you beside it may be nothing but the protest of a task that has not yet been taken up. The ordinary virtues cannot pay the debt of the extraordinary. Ask yourself what you are leaving undone by being so thoroughly in order. But be honest, for there is a cheaper explanation: a conscience trained by others, by parents, priests, neighbors, to bark whenever you step outside their approval. Test which it is. Does the guilt follow when you fear disapproval, or when you betray your own unfinished work? The first is a leash. The second is a summons.
I'd like to know why someone who does everything right may still have a bad conscience.

Because "right" is measured by the rule, and the rule was written for everyone. He who does everything right has satisfied the herd's ledger, which is a very cheap ledger; his conscience, however, may keep another. There is in some a task that no rule has named, a demand that speaks in a voice too low to be quoted, and this demand is exceptional because it is addressed to *him* alone. So he fulfils every duty, pays every debt, offends no custom, and still feels guilty, like a man who has answered all the questions on the examination save the one he was born to be asked.

Do not call this morbid. A bad conscience of this kind is often the last honest organ left in a man who has been praised too easily. Decent conduct becomes a hiding place; the applause of the neighbours is a soft bed. The unease says: you are being proper where you ought to be *necessary*. That is not a verdict against him. It is a summons.
Who is king among the blind?

The one who hears best. Where the sun is withheld from everyone, rank goes to the faculty that still functions, and so the king of the blind is the man with the longest ears. I once heard it from an old confessor who had gone deaf: we have eyes also in order to hear with them, he said, and he had spent a lifetime reading the trembling of lips and the flicker of shame in faces that could not bring themselves to speak.

Do not take this for mere wit. Every kingdom is a kingdom of the deprived. The one who rules does not see more than the others; he compensates more cunningly, he turns his one remaining sense into a scepter. The blind obey whoever tells them what is happening in the dark, and whoever tells them is always somewhat a liar, for he too is listening only to echoes.

Whoever would be king among the blind should therefore ask himself, with some shame, whether he wishes to be a king or to see.
Explain what the old deaf confessor said.

The old confessor, made deaf by a lifetime of listening, could still practice his art, for what he had lost at the ear he gained at the eye. Anyone who has sat through confessions knows that the words are the least of it; men say the lie and show the truth in the same breath. A trembling hand, a glance that slides away, a face that stiffens at precisely the wrong sin: these confess more than the tongue dares. So he hears with his eyes, and hears better than before.

And his second saying is crueler, and wiser. Among the blind, the one with the longest ears is king. Where others can perceive nothing, whoever perceives a little rules. Such is the power of the priest, and of every soul-tamer: he need not see far, only farther than the flock, only hear what they themselves have not learned to listen for in their own hearts. The kingdom of the confessor is built on the general deafness of men to themselves.
What is obstinacy called when it holds to a questionable cause?

It is called *loyalty*. Such is the vanity of the human heart that it gives its stubbornness the most honorable name in its vocabulary. A man holds fast to a cause whose questionableness has long since become obvious, perhaps to everyone but himself; he would have to admit an error, and to admit an error he would have to be a smaller man than he has told himself he is. So he clings, and he baptizes the clinging a virtue. Observe how much more flattering the word is: he who abandons a doubtful cause is called fickle, a deserter; he who stays by it, though he no longer believes in it, is called constant. Yet constancy is no merit in itself. A man may be constant in folly as faithfully as in wisdom. What the sentimental call loyalty is often only pride in its Sunday clothes, the refusal to let one's past selves be shown up as mistaken. I respect the man who can say, "I was wrong, and I leave"; he has the harder virtue.
I'd like to know what obstinacy calls itself.

It calls itself *loyalty*. That is the most flattering name in the vocabulary, and obstinacy has never been above borrowing a good coat. A man has defended some cause for years; then the cause begins to reveal its cracks, and every honest eye can see them, his own among them. To let go now would mean admitting that he was mistaken, and that he spent his best years, and perhaps his pride, on a doubtful thing. That is a bitter draught. So he does not let go. He grips harder, the harder the grip becomes to justify, and when asked why, he answers with a virtue: "I remain faithful."

But true loyalty is the fidelity of a free heart that tests what it loves and chooses it again. The obstinate man no longer chooses; he merely cannot bear the shame of having chosen wrongly. Loyalty to a cause that has become questionable is, more often than not, loyalty to one's own vanity, wearing the cause as a mask.
What is the prelude to science?

The prelude to science is *magic*, and all that foolish, feverish company of sorcerers, alchemists, astrologers and witches. Do you believe that knowledge would ever have arisen out of mere prudence, out of a sober curiosity that asked only for what could be had at once? Never! A thirst had first to be created, a hunger for *hidden and forbidden* powers, and for that, infinitely more had to be promised than could ever be kept. Only because the gold-makers swore to transmute lead, and the stargazers to read destiny, did men learn to crave what lay behind things; and in the long vain labor of fulfilling nothing, a little was at last fulfilled. Science is the sober heir of a great deception, and it should not be ashamed of its debauched ancestors.

Perhaps religion, too, will one day look like such a prelude, though it never knew itself as one: a schooling in longing, in which man learned to hunger and thirst, and finally to draw his own fullness out of himself.
Explain what magic and religion did for science.

Ask yourself whether the sciences would ever have grown had there not been sorcerers, alchemists, astrologers and witches before them. Those people had first to create a thirst, a hunger, a taste for *hidden and forbidden* powers. And to do this they had to promise infinitely more than could ever be kept, so that a little might at last be kept in the realm of knowledge. The lie was the seed-bed of the truth. Nobody digs for years after a modest fact; men will dig only for gold, for immortality, for the secret of the stars.

Religion, too, may one day look like a schooling of this kind, though no priest ever practised it as such. It taught man to feel, for once, the whole self-satisfaction of a God and all his power of self-redemption. Would man have learned to track down his own hunger and thirst, and to draw fullness out of himself, without that long apprenticeship? Prometheus had first to *imagine* that he stole the light and must do penance for the theft, in order to discover at last that he had made the light by longing for it.
Can someone whose plans keep failing still be happy?

Why should happiness depend on the plan succeeding? That is the assumption hidden in your question, and it is a petty one. The man whose plans keep failing is unhappy only if he has made his plans the measure of his life, if he believes that what he *wanted* was the sum of what was worth having. Some learn otherwise. After being brought several times to the abyss, such a man stops taking his wishes so seriously. He says: if this does not succeed, perhaps that will; and I may owe more to my failures than to my successes.

I would go further. Failure is an education in life that success rarely gives. He who has been on the point of losing everything knows what life weighs, and therefore *has* more of it than the cautious and the triumphant. He learns to improvise, to take the accident, the broken note, and work it into the music with a fine meaning.

So yes, such a person can be happy, provided they have found the worth of life somewhere other than in getting their way.
Compare two happy men, one who improvises well and one whose plans always fail.

Two kinds of fortune, and I would not trade either for the other's misery. The first man improvises: he takes the accident, the slip of the finger, the stray note, and makes it serve the whole. The world credits him with infallibility, though he errs like any mortal; his gift is that no error stays an error in his hands. He turns it into meaning. That is an art, and a rare one.

The second man is stranger, and I confess I love him more. Every design of his ends in ruin, and yet he is not wretched. Why? Because long ago he ceased to take his own wishes so seriously. He does not wear the bull's horns; he does not butt his head against the wall and call it will. He has stood so often at the edge of the abyss that he knows life from the inside, knows its taste as one knows only what one has nearly lost. Where the first man is rich in skill, this one is rich in *depth*. He thanks his failures more than his successes, and he has more life than those who never risked it.
Why do people honour priestly natures as wise?

Because the multitude is in need, and gratitude passes itself off as admiration. What the people call wisdom is reliability: a man who does not shift, who does not storm, who stands there gentle and serious and chaste, and who is therefore safe to be near. Set beside their own unreliability, such a man looks like a sage.

And consider what he does for them. He is the man before whom anyone may pour out his heart with impunity. The one who confesses gets rid of himself; he who has told his secret forgets it. There is a need for sewers and cleansing waters even for spiritual filth, and the priest is that hidden plumbing, a kind of non-public health-department of the soul. He sacrifices himself to be the vessel, a human sacrifice for the cleanliness of the rest.

So they honour him, and they are a thousand times justified. But do not call it wisdom in my sense. The thinker who lives in the storm-cloud of the highest problems is no comfort to anyone. The people bless the one who relieves them, and they crown that relief with the name of wisdom.
Explain why philosophers and the people disagree about what wisdom is.

They do not disagree about one thing; they are using one word for two needs. The people want from wisdom what a sick man wants from a nurse, or a sinner from a confessional: a place to set down their burden, someone steady and meek who will not judge, who will listen and forget. So they call "wise" the placid, pious man who gazes at life like a cow in a meadow, chewing it over with a serious face. They are not wrong to venerate him. He is a kind of sewer for the spirit, a pure current that carries away the filth of secrets and cares, and he pays for it with himself; the priest is a human sacrifice. They call him wise because he is reliable, and they are not.

The philosopher means something else entirely. He lives in the storm-cloud of the highest problems and the heaviest responsibilities, and there is no gazing there, no security, no indifference. His wisdom is a passion, not a comfort. No wonder the two cannot agree: one offers relief, the other offers danger.
Why do philosophers not regard the priest as a sage?

Because the philosopher has long ceased to believe in "sages," and he smells the people in that very belief. The word itself is a piece of popular faith: the crowd wants a being who *possesses* wisdom, finished and handed down like an heirloom, a man with a halo who can tell it what to do and what to fear. The priest supplies exactly this, and so the priest belongs to the people; he is their finest product and their most devoted servant, however loftily he may stand in the pulpit.

The philosopher knows how little of wisdom a man can have, and how much of that little is merely the fear of being without any. Think how the word came into the world in Greece. It was a *modesty* that coined "philosopher," a lover of wisdom, one who is underway and does not claim to have arrived; and it left the grand title "wise" to the play-actors of the spirit. A strange modesty, to be sure, in men like Pythagoras and Plato, who were monsters of pride and self-glorification. Their pride was so great that it could afford the humble word. The priest's humility is cheaper: he merely lends it out.
Help me understand why the priest is not a sage to philosophers.

Because the philosopher has a nose for the people, and he smells them even in the priest's robe. The priest believes in sages; he needs the word and the veneration that goes with it, since his whole trade lives on the faith of the many. But to the philosopher, this very faith in "the wise man" is already the crowd's superstition. Whoever believes in sages still belongs to the herd, however tall his hat, however solemn his Latin. The priest is not above the people but their most skillful voice, the one who gives their needs a holy name.

Notice, too, how the Greeks behaved. They did not call their thinkers "wise"; that proud title they left to the play-actors of the spirit. "Philosopher," a lover of wisdom, a seeker who does not yet possess, was invented out of modesty. Yet what monstrous pride hid in that modesty, in a Pythagoras, in a Plato! They refused the crown because they wanted no one's permission to wear it. The priest takes the title the crowd hands him; the philosopher is too proud to accept what the crowd can give.
What is great healthiness?

Great healthiness is not the absence of illness; that is the dream of the invalid and the ideal of the hospital. It is a health that one does not merely possess but must constantly *acquire*, because one constantly spends it again. The man who wants to circumnavigate every coast of the ideal, who wants to know from his own experience how it feels to be saint and scholar, artist and conqueror, cannot do it on a small and comfortable constitution. He will be shipwrecked, he will be wounded, he will be poisoned by things that would kill the timid. And he must have the strength to recover from all of it, again and again, and to come back from each wreck sharper, tougher, merrier than before.

So it is a health that can afford sickness, that uses its fevers as instruments of knowledge. Dangerous health, then, and I say so gladly. The merely safe are not healthy; they are only unexposed.
Tell me what great healthiness is and why the seeker of many ideals needs it.

Great healthiness is not the absence of illness, as the comfortable imagine. That is merely the health of the cow. I mean a health that is not only possessed but continually *won*, because it is continually spent, even squandered, in the venture. Whoever wants to sail around the whole inland sea of human ideals, who wants to know from his own body and soul what it is to be the saint, the artist, the legislator, the scholar, the devotee, will be shipwrecked again and again. Each ideal tries him like a fever; each one, lived through honestly and not merely described, takes something from him. He must therefore have a constitution that can be wounded, poisoned, even shattered, and then grow back stronger, sharper, more cheerful. Such a one is dangerously healthy: he recovers from what would kill another, and is richer for the sickness.

Why does the seeker need it? Because the many ideals are not to be *judged* from a chair; they must be *endured*. Only one who can lose his health and find it again may taste them all, and so stand beyond them.
What is the ideal of the spirit that plays naively with everything holy?

It is an ideal I name reluctantly, for it is full of danger, and I would not press it on anyone; one cannot hand another a *right* to it. I mean a spirit that plays, and plays *naively*: not from malice or mockery, but involuntarily, out of an overflowing abundance and power. To such a spirit everything that mankind has hitherto called holy, good, inviolable, divine is a toy, or at most a mild danger: a place where one might grow slack, blind, forgetful of oneself for an hour. What the people have laboriously set up as their highest measure of value, this spirit merely steps across.

Set beside all earlier seriousness, its goodness and well-being, superhuman in a human way, will look *inhuman*; it will seem the truest involuntary parody of every solemn gesture, word, tone, and morality the earth has known. And yet, I suspect, precisely there the great seriousness first begins. The real question mark is planted, the fate of the soul turns, the hand of the clock moves, and tragedy commences.
Describe the ideal of a spirit that plays with everything holy.

It is a strange and tempting ideal, and a dangerous one, which I would not press upon anyone, since I do not readily grant anyone the *right* to it. Picture a spirit that plays with everything hitherto called holy, good, inviolable, divine, and plays *naively*: not out of spite, not as a scoffer, but involuntarily, from an overflow of abundance and power. Such a spirit does not profane the holy; it simply has too much health to be bound by it. What the people, reasonably enough, take as their highest measure of value would seem to it a danger, a relaxation, a blindness, a moment of self-forgetfulness.

To all the solemn ones, this spirit must look inhuman. Set beside the whole long earnestness of the past, its gestures, its tone, its look, its morality, it resembles a parody, the truest and most involuntary parody of it. And yet I suspect that with this very figure the *great seriousness* first begins. Only then is the question mark truly set up, only then does the soul's fate turn, the hour-hand move, and tragedy *begin*.
